topics.title: Chemical Reactions and Chemical Equations
topics.content_text:
A complete chemical equation represents the reactants, products and their physical states symbolically. A chemical reaction has occurred if there is a change in state, change in colour, evolution of a gas, or change in temperature. For example, when zinc granules are added to dilute sulphuric acid in a conical flask, bubbles of hydrogen gas are evolved and the flask becomes warm.

$$\text{Zn (s)} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{ (aq)} \longrightarrow \text{ZnSO}_4\text{ (aq)} + \text{H}_2\text{ (g)} \uparrow$$

According to the Law of Conservation of Mass, the total mass of the elements present in the products of a chemical reaction has to be equal to the total mass of the elements present in the reactants. Hence, equations must be balanced by equalising the number of atoms of each element on both sides.

topics.title: Types of Chemical Reactions
topics.content_text:
Chemical reactions involve the breaking and making of bonds between atoms to produce new substances. The primary types of chemical reactions include:
1. Combination Reaction: When two or more substances combine to form a single product. E.g., burning of coal: $\text{C (s)} + \text{O}_2\text{ (g)} \rightarrow \text{CO}_2\text{ (g)}$.
2. Decomposition Reaction: A single reactant breaks down into simpler products when energy is supplied in the form of heat, light, or electricity.
3. Displacement Reaction: A more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its salt solution. E.g., $\text{Fe} + \text{CuSO}_4 \rightarrow \text{FeSO}_4 + \text{Cu}$.
4. Double Displacement Reaction: Reactions where there is an exchange of ions between the reactants. E.g., $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{BaCl}_2 \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4 \downarrow + 2\text{NaCl}$.

topics.title: Oxidation, Reduction, Corrosion and Rancidity
topics.content_text:
Corrosion: When a metal is attacked by substances around it such as moisture, acids, and oxygen, it is said to corrode, and this process is called corrosion. Common examples include the reddish brown coating on iron (rusting, $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 \cdot x\text{H}_2\text{O}$), the black coating on silver (silver sulphide, $\text{Ag}_2\text{S}$), and the green coating on copper (basic copper carbonate, $\text{CuCO}_3 \cdot \text{Cu(OH)}_2$).

Rancidity: When fats and oils are oxidised, they become rancid and their smell and taste change. Usually substances which prevent oxidation (antioxidants) are added to foods containing fats and oil. Keeping food in airtight containers helps to slow down oxidation. Chips manufacturers usually flush bags of chips with gas such as nitrogen to prevent the oil from getting oxidised.

topics.title: Reflection of Light
topics.content_text:
Light seems to travel along straight lines in transparent media. The fact that a small source of light casts a sharp shadow of an opaque object points to this straight-line path of light, usually indicated as a ray of light.

Laws of Reflection of Light:
1. The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection: $\angle i = \angle r$.
2. The incident ray, the normal to the mirror at the point of incidence and the reflected ray, all lie in the same plane.
These laws of reflection are applicable to all types of reflecting surfaces including spherical surfaces. Image formed by a plane mirror is always virtual and erect. The size of the image is equal to that of the object. The image formed is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it, and is laterally inverted.

topics.title: Refraction of Light
topics.content_text:
The reflecting surface of a spherical mirror may be curved inwards or outwards. A spherical mirror whose reflecting surface is curved inwards, that is, faces towards the centre of the sphere, is called a concave mirror. A spherical mirror whose reflecting surface is curved outwards is called a convex mirror.

Mirror Formula:
$$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u}$$
where $u$ is object distance, $v$ is image distance, and $f$ is focal length.

Magnification ($m$):
$$m = \frac{\text{Height of image } (h')}{\text{Height of object } (h)} = -\frac{v}{u}$$
A negative sign in the value of magnification indicates that the image is real. A positive sign indicates that the image is virtual.

topics.content_text: All matter is composed of atoms and molecules. The electric charge is an intrinsic property of elementary particles like electrons and protons. topics.title: Electric Field & Electric Dipole
topics.content_text:
Coulomb's Law states that the electrical force between two stationary point charges $q_1$ and $q_2$ in vacuum is directly proportional to the product of their magnitudes and inversely proportional to the square of the distance $r$ separating them:

$$\vec{F}_{12} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2} \hat{r}_{12}$$

where $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{C}^2\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^{-2}$ is the permittivity of free space. In a dielectric medium with relative permittivity $\varepsilon_r$, the force reduces to $F = F_0 / \varepsilon_r$.

topics.title: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
topics.content_text:
Gauss's Law states that the total electric flux $\Phi_E$ through any closed surface $S$ is equal to $1/\varepsilon_0$ times the total net charge enclosed inside that closed surface:

$$\Phi_E = \oint_S \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{Q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0}$$

Applications include deriving the electric field due to an infinitely long uniformly charged wire ($E = \lambda / (2\pi\varepsilon_0 r)$), an infinite uniform plane sheet of charge ($E = \sigma / (2\varepsilon_0)$), and a thin spherical shell.

4. Fringe Width expression: β = λD/d; Equal spacing of dark and bright fringes
5. Effect of changing variables: dipping apparatus in water (β' = β/μ), changing slit separation d, white light central white fringe

topics.content_text:

5. Quantized Energy Expression: E_n = -13.6 / n² eV

topics.title: Concentration Terms & Solubility
topics.content_text: Solutions are homogeneous mixtures of two or more than two components. The concentration of a solution may be expressed quantitatively as mass percentage, volume percentage, parts per million (ppm), mole fraction ($x$), molarity ($M$), or molality ($m$). Henry's Law states that at a constant temperature, the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of the gas present above the surface of liquid or solution ($p = K_H \cdot x$).

topics.title: Vapour Pressure & Raoult's Law
topics.content_text: Raoult's Law for volatile liquids states that for a solution of volatile liquids, the partial vapour pressure of each component of the solution is directly proportional to its mole fraction present in solution ($p_1 = p_1^0 x_1$). Colligative properties depend only on the number of solute particles and not on their nature. These include relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point ($\Delta T_b = K_b m$), depression of freezing point ($\Delta T_f = K_f m$), and osmotic pressure ($\Pi = CRT$).

topics.title: Colligative Properties & Van 't Hoff Factor
topics.content_text:
This section covers the canonical NCERT curriculum for Colligative Properties & Van 't Hoff Factor in the chapter "Solutions".

Key Concepts Covered:
1. Relative Lowering of Vapour Pressure (RLVP): (p°_A - p_A)/p°_A = i · x_B ≈ i (w_B M_A / M_B w_A)
2. Elevation in Boiling Point: ΔT_b = i · K_b · m (K_b = molal elevation constant / ebullioscopic constant)
3. Depression in Freezing Point: ΔT_f = i · K_f · m (K_f = molal depression constant / cryoscopic constant)
4. Osmotic Pressure (Π): Π = i · CRT = i (n_B/V)RT; Isotonic, Hypertonic, and Hypotonic solutions; Reverse Osmosis (RO)
5. Why osmotic pressure is preferred for biomolecules/polymers (room temperature, uses molarity, measurable magnitudes)
6. Van 't Hoff factor (i) = Normal molar mass / Observed molar mass = Total moles after / Initial moles
7. Degree of Dissociation: α = (i - 1)/(n - 1); Degree of Association: α = (1 - i)/(1 - 1/n)

topics.title: Preparation and Reactions of K₂Cr₂O₇ and KMnO₄
topics.content_text:
This section covers the canonical NCERT curriculum for Preparation and Reactions of K₂Cr₂O₇ and KMnO₄ in the chapter "The d- and f-Block Elements".

Key Concepts Covered:
1. Potassium Dichromate (K₂Cr₂O₇): Preparation from Chromite ore (FeCr₂O₄) via Na₂CrO₄ and Na₂Cr₂O₇
2. pH-dependent interconversion: 2CrO₄²⁻ (yellow) + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange) + H₂O
3. Oxidizing actions in acid: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O (oxidizes I⁻ → I₂, Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺, H₂S → S, Sn²⁺ → Sn⁴⁺)
4. Potassium Permanganate (KMnO₄): Preparation from Pyrolusite ore (MnO₂) via green K₂MnO₄
5. Oxidizing actions in acid: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O (oxidizes Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺, C₂O₄²⁻ → CO₂, I⁻ → I₂)
6. Oxidizing actions in neutral/faintly alkaline: MnO₄⁻ + 2H₂O + 3e⁻ → MnO₂ + 4OH⁻ (oxidizes I⁻ → IO₃⁻ iodate)

topics.title: Bonding Theories (Werner, VBT, CFT)
topics.content_text:
This section covers the canonical NCERT curriculum for Bonding Theories (Werner, VBT, CFT) in the chapter "Coordination Compounds".

Key Concepts Covered:
1. Werner's Theory: Primary valency (ionizable, oxidation state) vs Secondary valency (non-ionizable, coordination number)
2. Valence Bond Theory (VBT): sp³ (Tetrahedral), dsp² (Square planar), sp³d² (Outer orbital, high spin), d²sp³ (Inner orbital, low spin)
3. VBT limitations: Cannot explain color, spectra, or relative ligand strength
4. Crystal Field Theory (CFT): Octahedral field splitting into lower t_2g (-0.4 Δ_o) and upper e_g (+0.6 Δ_o)
5. Spectrochemical Series: I⁻ < Br⁻ < S²⁻ < Cl⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < C₂O₄²⁻ < H₂O < NCS⁻ < EDTA⁴⁻ < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO
6. High spin (Δ_o < P, weak field) vs Low spin (Δ_o > P, strong field) configurations for d⁴ to d⁷ ions
7. Tetrahedral Field Splitting: Δ_t = (4/9) Δ_o; Pairing energy P > Δ_t always (high spin complexes)
8. Color mechanism: d-d electronic transition across Δ_o absorbing complementary light

4. Electrophilic substitution in haloarenes: Halogens are deactivating but ortho/para directing due to +R overriding -I at o/p

topics.content_text:

topics.content_text:

topics.title: Distinguishing Tests & Carbonyl Named Reactions
topics.content_text:
This section covers the canonical NCERT curriculum for Distinguishing Tests & Carbonyl Named Reactions in the chapter "Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids".

Key Concepts Covered:
1. Tollens’ Test (Silver Mirror): Positive for all aldehydes (aliphatic and aromatic); R-CHO + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + 3OH⁻ → R-COO⁻ + 2Ag↓ + 4NH₃ + 2H₂O
2. Fehling’s Test: Positive for aliphatic aldehydes (red Cu₂O precipitate); Aromatic aldehydes and ketones fail
3. Iodoform Test (I₂ + NaOH): Positive for CH₃-C=O and CH₃-CH(OH)- groups (ethanal, all methyl ketones, ethanol, propan-2-ol); yields bright yellow CHI₃ precipitate
4. Aldol Condensation: Carbonyls with α-hydrogen with dilute NaOH yield β-hydroxyaldehyde (aldol) which dehydrates on heating to α,β-unsaturated carbonyl
5. Cannizzaro Reaction: Aldehydes lacking α-hydrogen (HCHO, PhCHO) with 50% conc. NaOH disproportionate into alcohol and carboxylic acid salt
6. Clemmensen Reduction: >C=O + Zn-Hg + conc. HCl → >CH₂; Wolff-Kishner Reduction: >C=O + NH₂NH₂ / KOH / ethylene glycol, Δ → >CH₂ + N₂

topics.title: Carboxylic Acids: Acidity & Reactions
topics.content_text:
This section covers the canonical NCERT curriculum for Carboxylic Acids: Acidity & Reactions in the chapter "Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids".

Key Concepts Covered:
1. Acidity of Carboxylic Acids: Higher than phenols because carboxylate ion stabilizes negative charge equally over two electronegative oxygen atoms
2. Substituent effects: EWG (-NO₂, -CN, -F, -Cl) increase acidity; EDG decrease acidity (CF₃COOH > CCl₃COOH > CHCl₂COOH > NO₂CH₂COOH > HCOOH > PhCOOH > CH₃COOH)
3. Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction: Carboxylic acids with α-hydrogen react with Cl₂/Br₂ and red P to yield α-halocarboxylic acids
4. Decarboxylation: Sodium salts of carboxylic acids heated with soda-lime (NaOH + CaO 3:1) yield alkane with one fewer carbon

topics.title: Basicity of Amines
topics.content_text:
This section covers the canonical NCERT curriculum for Basicity of Amines in the chapter "Amines".

Key Concepts Covered:
1. Gas phase basicity: 3° > 2° > 1° > NH₃ (governed purely by +I electron-donating effect)
2. Aqueous phase basicity: Interplay of inductive, hydration energy (H-bonding), and steric hindrance
3. Methyl-substituted in water: 2° > 1° > 3° > NH₃ [(CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > (CH₃)₃N > NH₃]
4. Ethyl-substituted in water: 2° > 3° > 1° > NH₃ [(C₂H₅)₂NH > (C₂H₅)₃N > C₂H₅NH₂ > NH₃]
5. Basicity of Aniline: Aniline is a weaker base than ammonia and aliphatic amines because nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the benzene ring via resonance

topics.content_text:
This section covers the canonical NCERT curriculum for Carbohydrates: Glucose Structure & Polysaccharides in the chapter "Biomolecules".

topics.title: Introduction
topics.content_text: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic states that every composite number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique, apart from the order in which the prime factors occur. For any two positive integers $a$ and $b$, $\text{HCF}(a, b) \times \text{LCM}(a, b) = a \times b$. We use this theorem to prove that numbers such as $\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$, and $\sqrt{5}$ are irrational numbers.

topics.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
topics.content_text: A polynomial of degree 1 is called a linear polynomial, degree 2 is quadratic, and degree 3 is cubic. For a quadratic polynomial $ax^2 + bx + c$, if $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the zeroes, then $\alpha + \beta = -b/a$ and $\alpha\beta = c/a$. The zeroes are the $x$-coordinates of the points where the graph of $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ intersects the $x$-axis.
